# 032 · A batch listener that commits the whole batch after a failed record loses the rest of it

[← All examples](../README.md)

| Verdict | Categories | Severity if shipped | Change | Verified unit | Approach |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **✗ Violation: counterexample found** | functional | critical | bug-fix, behaviour change intended | [`BatchCommit#offsetToCommit`](../../examples/apps/crosscut/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/crosscut/kafka/BatchCommit.java) | [B11: Property proofs](../../lib/README.md) |

> A batch listener commits one past the last record it finished: the whole batch when every record is done, the failed record's own offset when one is not, so that it and everything after it come back. An on-call engineer, after a night of a consumer re-reading a poison batch, makes the listener commit the batch whatever happened, and updates the test to match. The module's properties file states what a committed offset means, and the prover refutes the change with a batch whose failed record is not its last.

Tags: [messaging](../README.md#tag-messaging)

## The change

Commit `batchStart + batchSize` regardless of the failed record. The reasoning: the failed record is logged and alerted on, and holding the batch back for it redelivers the batch forever when the record is poison. The test that expected the commit to stop at the failed record is changed to expect the whole batch, and the suite passes.

**Before** ([`BatchCommit.java`](../../examples/apps/crosscut/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/crosscut/kafka/BatchCommit.java), line 21):

```java
        if (batchStart < 0 || batchSize <= 0 || failedIndex < NONE_FAILED || failedIndex >= batchSize) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("batchStart >= 0, batchSize > 0 and -1 <= failedIndex < batchSize are required");
        }
        return failedIndex == NONE_FAILED ? batchStart + batchSize : batchStart + failedIndex;
    }
}
```

**After:**

```java
        if (batchStart < 0 || batchSize <= 0 || failedIndex < NONE_FAILED || failedIndex >= batchSize) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("batchStart >= 0, batchSize > 0 and -1 <= failedIndex < batchSize are required");
        }
        // A failed record is logged and alerted on. Holding the batch back for it redelivers the batch forever
        // when the record is poison, so commit the batch whatever happened.
        return batchStart + batchSize;
    }
}
```

## What the verifier found

The property `result >= batchStart && result <= batchStart + batchSize && (failedIndex == -1 ? result == batchStart + batchSize : result == batchStart + failedIndex)` does not hold on every input where `batchStart >= 0 && batchStart <= 4611686018427387903L && batchSize > 0 && batchSize <= 100000 && failedIndex >= -1 && failedIndex < batchSize` holds. The prover found this input, and the tool replayed it on the method to show what it does:

| Input | The method's outcome |
|---|---|
| `offsetToCommit(batchStart=0, batchSize=1, failedIndex=0)` | `1` |

One input is enough to fail the build. The domain is `batchStart: long × batchSize: int × failedIndex: int`; the search tries small values first so that the witness is readable, and would have covered all of it.

## Would the existing tests have caught it?

No: every existing unit test passes (`java -ea net.terminalvalue.crosscut.Tests`, run against the patched code).

## Why it matters

In a batch of five hundred records where the third fails, the listener stops at the third: the other four hundred and ninety-seven were never processed. Committing past the batch marks them as read, and the consumer never sees them again. They are not in a dead-letter topic, because only the failed record was reported; they are simply gone, from the consumer's point of view, and the first sign is a reconciliation job weeks later. The poison-batch loop that prompted the change is real, and Spring Kafka's answer to it is to retry the failed record a bounded number of times and then dead-letter it, which commits past it without losing the rest. The change fixed the symptom by removing the at-least-once guarantee of every batch that ever has a failure.

## Why the verdict is right

The property is the one sentence of Kafka's commit semantics: the committed offset is the next record to read, so it is one past the batch when every record is done and the failed record itself when one is not, never further and never short. The patched method violates the second clause on the smallest input with a failure: a batch of one record at offset zero whose record failed, for which it commits one instead of zero, so the failed record itself is marked as read. The tool replays it. The updated test cannot see the problem, because it was updated to agree with the code; the property was not written by the person making the change, and states what every listener must do.

## What to do

Revert, and fix the poison-batch loop where Spring Kafka fixes it: a `DefaultErrorHandler` with a bounded back-off and a `DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer`, which retries the failed record and then publishes it to a dead-letter topic, after which the commit moves past it legitimately. The property stays in the file: a later change to this line is checked against every batch shape, including the ones no test enumerates.
